The premise that biological systems can only be understood by simultaneously interrogating multiple molecular layers has, in little more than a decade, moved from methodological aspiration to routine expectation. A single study now routinely combines genomic, transcriptomic, epigenomic, proteomic and metabolomic assays, often at single-cell or spatial resolution, and with metagenomic, metatranscriptomic and metaproteomic layers when the system of interest is a microbial community [R1, R54, R60]. Each layer is generated by a different assay, preprocessed by a different toolchain and stored in a different format, with sample overlap that is rarely complete and with technical noise that is not comparable across modalities [R1]. The heterogeneity is not cosmetic: it determines which statistical operations are even defined, and propagates through every downstream decision about imputation, normalisation, dimension reduction and testing. The community has produced a correspondingly heterogeneous software landscape, and the practical question for working scientists is no longer whether to integrate but which stack to adopt.

That choice has become harder because the algorithm catalogue has fragmented along several largely independent axes. Unsupervised latent-factor approaches such as Multi-Omics Factor Analysis infer shared and modality-specific variation [R2], and the same conceptual core has been carried into single-cell profiling [R4] and transfer-learning extensions [R42], with the MOFA2 release line representing the actively maintained successor whose broader bulk/single-cell behaviour is not separately characterised in the cited evidence. Matrix-factorisation methods for incomplete multi-omics blocks have been added to the catalogue [R13], while parallel network-based meta-analytic frameworks now unify statistical aggregation with similarity-network-fusion-style integration [R6]. A separate longitudinal literature models repeated measurements of the same subjects [R27, R28], and pathway-aware tools offer functional priors as a route to factor interpretation [R32, R20]. A parallel deep-learning literature frames integration as representation learning rather than decomposition [R8, R9, R19, R23, R39, R44], and the single-cell regime has generated its own dedicated probabilistic and graph-linked ecosystems, including scVI and its semi-supervised extension scANVI [R61, R62] and totalVI for paired RNA and surface protein measurements [R63]. Web-based platforms wrap subsets of these algorithms behind point-and-click interfaces [R10, R14, R15, R49, R50], while reproducibly containerised pipelines package yet other subsets for command-line execution [R18, R21]. Data structure convergence around MultiAssayExperiment [R36] and its single-cell counterpart [R51] is partial; file conventions and evaluation metrics remain heterogeneous across the tools reviewed, so applying several methods to the same dataset typically requires substantial engineering effort [R7].

Microbiome research sharpens every one of these difficulties. A meaningful study must coordinate at least four interacting layers — the microbial community, its viruses, its host and the metabolic exchange between them — each profilable by multiple assays with non-overlapping sample sets [R1, R54]. Disease-focused work in type 2 diabetes illustrates the gap: reproducible metagenomic signatures can be linked to functional pathways and metabolites, but the chain from genetic potential to expressed activity to host phenotype depends on whether metabolomic, metatranscriptomic and proteomic measurements were obtained on the same individuals [R57]. Pipelines such as gNOMO and gNOMO2 address part of this problem for amplicon, metagenomic, metatranscriptomic and metaproteomic data with and without host context [R21, R34], and microbiome-aware multi-omics workflows built on standardised R/Bioconductor classes align the microbial and host sides of the problem [R1]. Even so, the field lacks a consensus benchmark, and the dominant reviews do not yet agree on what a successful integration should demonstrate.

A further, often underappreciated, dimension is that integration is not solely a statistical question. The reproducibility crisis in computational biology has shown that the same algorithm, executed by two groups on nominally the same data, can yield qualitatively different results, with the principal sources of divergence being software versions, parameter choices and undocumented preprocessing rather than the mathematical core of the method. FAIR-compliant packaging of multi-omics workflows as Research Object Crates [R18], curated simulators such as SUMO for controlled evaluation [R11], single-cell multi-omics benchmarks across 47 datasets [R17] and comparative studies of 12 integration methods on joint scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq tasks [R48] have emerged in response. These efforts reveal that the binding constraint on the field is engineering and infrastructure: data structures such as MultiAssayExperiment [R36] and its single-cell counterpart [R51], containerised workflow managers and provenance metadata determine which analyses are even tractable before statistical sophistication is brought to bear.

Existing reviews of multi-omics software tend to conflate three quite different objects — algorithms, packages and end-to-end workflows — within a single list, and to evaluate them by features rather than by behaviour on common data [R60]. The consequence is that a reader finishes such a review no better equipped to choose between, for instance, a deep-learning framework, a factor-analysis package and a microbiome-centred pipeline than before reading it. This review adopts a deliberately narrower ambition: it applies a common set of criteria — input data structures, handling of missingness, supervision, scalability, biological target, reproducibility infrastructure and empirical benchmarking — to a curated set of frameworks, packages, workflows and platforms, and uses those criteria to situate one microbiome-centred workflow as a featured example. The aim is not to crown a winner but to expose, through comparison, the engineering choices that quietly determine which scientific questions are answerable.

The term "multi-omics integration" is frequently invoked as though it referred to a single statistical operation, yet the algorithmic landscape encompasses fundamentally different commitments to the data-generating process. Methods as superficially similar as similarity-network fusion and matrix factorisation impose distinct assumptions about the distribution of signal across modalities, the nature of cross-platform concordance, and the role of prior biological knowledge, and a working taxonomy is required before any meaningful comparison of software tools can be undertaken. In what follows, I organise the field along three axes: the stage at which integration is performed (early, intermediate or late), the degree of supervision required (unsupervised, semi-supervised or supervised), and the biological target the analysis is designed to address (subtyping, biomarker selection, longitudinal modelling or dynamic network inference).

The most informative first axis is integration stage. Early integration concatenates normalised modality matrices into a single design matrix and applies standard multivariate or supervised methods, an approach implemented, for example, in PLS-based workflows within mixOmics [R3]. Concatenation preserves the original feature space but ignores modality-specific noise structure and is highly sensitive to differences in scale and feature cardinality. Intermediate integration builds a joint latent representation, either by factor-analytic decomposition as in Multi-Omics Factor Analysis [R2], MOTL [R42] and Multi-Layer Matrix Factorisation [R13], or by graph-based embedding as in SNF [R5], MODILM [R52] and MO-GCAN [R39]. Late, or decision-level, integration trains separate models on each modality and combines their outputs; deep learning frameworks such as DeepMoIC [R19] and MOADLN [R23] instantiate intermediate integration through latent representation fusion, with downstream classification heads that yield decision-level outputs. Crucially, these three strategies are not interchangeable: the choice of stage changes the failure modes of an analysis, and tools marketed under a single integration label frequently combine stages internally without disclosing the implications.

The second axis concerns supervision. Unsupervised factor-analytic methods dominate the literature precisely because matched multi-omics cohorts are usually too small to support fully labelled learning; MOFA infers shared and modality-specific latent factors without external labels and then enables downstream subtyping, imputation and outlier detection [R2], while mixOmics provides a continuum from unsupervised PLS variants to the supervised discriminant variant DIABLO [R3, R35]. Semi-supervised approaches explicitly leverage small labelled subsets alongside large unlabelled ones: SSD-MO combines deep non-negative matrix factorisation with a semi-supervised objective and was shown to improve clustering F-scores on six TCGA datasets [R9], although the extent to which these gains generalise beyond cancer subtyping has not been established. Fully supervised frameworks such as the network-based Bayesian method NetMIM [R20] and the graph-attention-based MODILM [R52] address biomarker selection and disease classification directly, but they depend on the existence of trustworthy endpoints and cannot answer exploratory questions about novel molecular strata.

The third axis, biological target, distinguishes tools whose statistical machinery is tailored to a specific scientific goal. Sample subtyping is the most heavily studied target: SNF fuses per-modality patient similarity networks and was reported to outperform single-modality analyses and several integration baselines across five cancer cohorts [R5], while MLMF extends factorisation to handle partial multi-omics matrices across twelve multi-omics datasets drawn from cancer studies [R13], and graph-attention and graph-convolutional approaches such as MO-GCAN [R39] and DeepMoIC [R19] target the same problem with neural architectures. Biomarker selection is the explicit objective of DIABLO [R35] and NetMIM [R20], the latter additionally accommodating block missingness through data augmentation. A more specialised target is longitudinal modelling, addressed by timeOmics [R27] and PALM [R31], with PALM aligning multi-omics time series before reconstructing dynamic Bayesian networks in an inflammatory bowel disease cohort [R31]. Dynamic network inference proper, the reconstruction of time-resolved regulatory graphs spanning omics layers, is the central aim of netOmics [R28] and PALM [R31], and is statistically distinct from subtyping even though both produce graphical outputs.

This three-axis taxonomy should not, however, be read as a neutral classification. The benchmarks available do not yet justify a confident ranking across stages: the single-cell integration benchmark of Hu and colleagues reports that Seurat, MOJITOO and scAI outperform other vertical-integration methods on most of the 47 datasets evaluated [R17], while a parallel benchmark of joint scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq integration finds that no single method dominates across tasks [R48], and neither study examines bulk multi-omics subtyping or longitudinal targets. Conflating similarity-network fusion with matrix factorisation obscures a real methodological contrast: SNF operates by fusing per-modality sample similarity networks [R5], whereas factor-analytic methods such as MOFA infer a small number of shared and modality-specific latent axes [R2], and empirical benchmarks to date have not formally distinguished these alternative data-generating assumptions. What the literature does not show is that any single axis dominates the others; integrative method choice must therefore be made conditional on the assumed data-generating process, the size and labelling of the cohort, and the specific biological question being asked, and software reviews that ignore these axes risk endorsing tools whose assumptions are violated by the very data they are applied to.

General-purpose integration frameworks occupy an unusual position in the multi-omics software landscape: they are not tied to a particular biological question or sample type, but instead supply statistical machinery that operates on whatever blocks the user supplies. Within the R/Bioconductor ecosystem, this category is anchored by the MultiAssayExperiment class, which provides a coordinated representation of diverse assays together with subsetting, reshaping and cross-assay aggregation primitives [R36]. MultiAssayExperiment does not enforce any particular model: it is an interchange format on top of which methods such as MOFA, mixOmics or pathway-based routines can be plugged in, and the SingleCellMultiModal Bioconductor package redistributes curated landmark CITE-seq, 10x Multiome and related datasets as MultiAssayExperiment objects to support method development on standardised inputs [R51].

The most visible statistical engines are the PLS-family methods consolidated in mixOmics, which provides sparse and discriminant variants for dimension reduction and feature selection across multiple 'omics blocks [R3]. DIABLO, the supervised extension implemented within the same package, seeks correlated discriminant features across data types and has been adopted for cancer case studies integrating mRNA, miRNA, CpG, protein and metabolite matrices [R35]. PLS-based methods are, by construction, linear and rely on cross-block covariance structure; in highly compositional or sparsity-dominated data, such as sparse microbiome count tables with many zeros and strong library-size effects, this construction can yield unstable loading signs and inflated cross-block correlations, so users are well advised to verify the linearity and correlation assumptions empirically before trusting cross-omics feature signatures. This limitation reflects the underlying PLS methodology rather than any specific shortcoming of the mixOmics implementation, and applies to any PLS-derived integrator rather than to mixOmics in particular.

Factor-analytic frameworks relax the assumption of correlated blocks by learning latent factors that can be shared or modality-specific. MOFA was introduced as an unsupervised probabilistic factor model for bulk multi-omics, providing sample subtyping, imputation and outlier detection via variational inference [R2]. The single-cell-focused MOFA+ generalised this formulation with scalable inference and flexible sparsity priors to handle multiple sample groups and modalities such as paired RNA and epigenetic profiling [R4]. These models offer probabilistic grounding and factor-level interpretability, but the documented case studies are limited to specific cancer settings [R2, R4]; whether MOFA-style factor inference generalises to the zero-inflated compositional distributions typical of microbiome relative abundance matrices, or how factor interpretability behaves as the number of modalities grows beyond three, remains, to our knowledge, untested in the cited primary literature. Extensions such as MOTL have begun to address limited-sample settings by transferring factor structure from larger datasets [R42], illustrating that active development of the MOFA family continues beyond the original publications and that conclusions drawn from the original MOFA and MOFA+ studies [R2, R4] should not be assumed to characterise the current maintained releases.

A different axis of generality is pursued by pathway-level integration tools. The pathwayMultiomics package provides a roll-up strategy that does not require matched samples and uses a novel MiniMax statistic to prioritise dysregulated pathways across categorical, continuous or survival outcomes [R32]. By aggregating features before integration, such methods trade the resolution of gene-level signals for robustness and interpretability; the available excerpt does not address how pathwayMultiomics handles the compositional structure that dominates microbiome data, where correlation networks at the pathway level can be driven by shared denominators rather than shared biology, so its applicability to compositional microbiome inputs should be regarded as untested rather than unsupported.

A fourth layer consists of wrapper pipelines that treat the proliferation of integration methods as a usability problem rather than a statistical one. moiraine automates preprocessing, input formatting, visualisation and side-by-side comparison of several integration tools on the same dataset [R7], while MUUMI unifies statistical meta-analysis with network-based integration, including similarity network fusion, to identify robust molecular signatures in IPF transcriptomic and macrophage multi-omics data [R6]. Neither wrapper ships with a Bayesian assessment of whether one integrated solution is genuinely better than another; they make comparison easier but do not adjudicate it. Similarly, SUMO provides controlled synthetic multi-omics data with user-defined latent structures [R11], yet the absence of a broadly adopted ground-truth corpus continues to limit head-to-head evaluation of competing methods on a level methodological playing field.

Taken together, the generalist frameworks provide a coordinated data infrastructure [R36, R51], two dominant inferential families with distinct theoretical foundations (PLS-based [R3, R35] and Bayesian factor-analytic [R2, R4]), and an emerging layer of comparison tooling and simulation infrastructure [R7, R6, R11]. What the present evidence does not establish is that any of these general-purpose stacks ship, by default, with the microbiome-specific preparation logic that dedicated microbiome workflows typically require; this gap is part of the motivation behind microbiome-flavoured workflows such as EasyMultiProfiler, which build on the same MultiAssayExperiment container and provide a module-oriented R interface (extraction, preparation, support, analysis, visualisation), illustrated on human and mouse gut host–microbiome datasets [R1]. The same caveat about absent head-to-head benchmarking applies symmetrically to the comparison frameworks discussed above [R7, R6, R11], and to the as-yet-unstated behaviour of MOFA-family factor models on microbiome inputs [R2, R4, R42].

Microbiome multi-omics occupies a distinctive niche within the broader integration landscape because the biological substrate—microbial communities sequenced at population scale—imposes constraints that generic statistical frameworks do not address. A 16S or metagenomic layer delivers a sparse, hierarchical count matrix whose units are operational taxonomic units, amplicon sequence variants or metagenome-assembled genomes, while metatranscriptomic, metaproteomic and host-response layers enter at incompatible resolutions, with markedly different missingness patterns and dynamic ranges [R54]. Few of the general-purpose frameworks discussed elsewhere in this review were designed to align these inputs, which has motivated a small but coherent set of microbiome-native tools.

The earliest of these is gNOMO, a Snakemake-based pipeline that explicitly targets non-model host-associated microbiomes and integrates up to three meta-omics layers (metagenomics, metatranscriptomics and metaproteomics) together with host or environmental context, demonstrated on the cockroach Blattella germanica [R34]. Its contribution was less the introduction of new statistical machinery than the recognition that reference databases for symbiont communities of non-model organisms are sparse and that integration must therefore accommodate partial annotation and host-derived contamination in the same workflow. gNOMO2, the modular Nextflow successor, generalises this approach to canonical model microbiomes, handles two to four omics combinations including 16S rRNA, metagenomics, metatranscriptomics and metaproteomics, and adds differential-abundance, integration and visualisation modules benchmarked on four datasets [R21]. Importantly, gNOMO2 is presented as a reproducible infrastructure layer rather than a statistical engine: it orchestrates established tools within a containerised pipeline and exposes integration-relevant outputs (matched feature tables, taxonomic roll-ups, functional projections) for downstream analysis, but it does not, by itself, propose a new integrative model.

A different design philosophy underlies PALM, a computational pipeline for longitudinal microbiome multi-omics that aligns time-resolved sequence, expression, metabolomic and host-transcriptomic data and reconstructs a unified model via dynamic Bayesian networks, with applications in inflammatory bowel disease [R31]. PALM's distinguishing feature is its explicit treatment of temporal misalignment between layers: differences in sampling cadence and progression rate across omics are handled through a biologically inspired alignment step before the dynamic network is fit. PALM therefore addresses a complementary problem to static integration frameworks, focusing on dynamic regulatory inference in longitudinal cohorts rather than cross-sectional feature association.

Outside human and insect hosts, dedicated integration infrastructure is thinner. In livestock, a recent methodological review argues that identifying keystone microbial taxa in ruminant and monogastric guts requires network-level integration of genomic, metabolic and host multi-omics data, but the tools it evaluates are predominantly general-purpose network or matrix-factorisation methods applied to microbial data rather than pipelines built natively for that purpose, and performance claims rest on cross-domain extrapolation in the absence of livestock-specific benchmarks [R58]. In clinical microbiome cohorts such as type 2 diabetes, integrative multi-omics has revealed consistent strain- and pathway-level signatures, yet most studies still rely on ad hoc combinations of metagenomic profiling, metatranscriptomics and metabolomics that are not packaged as reusable workflows; the bottleneck is no longer methodology but annotation, with strain-level resolution and host–microbe protein–metabolite linkage remaining difficult to standardise [R57]. A parallel observation emerges from the tuberculosis metabolomics literature, where low concordance of differential metabolites across human and animal models coexists with conserved pathway-level disruption, suggesting that integration frameworks without explicit pathway-mapping primitives will under-detect biologically aligned signal [R59].

Comparable gaps are evident in adjacent clinical and immunological domains where multi-omics is heavily used but infrastructure is underdeveloped. In exosomal cardiovascular biomarker discovery, reproducibility and validation gaps dominate despite an abundance of AI/ML integration methods, with ensemble classifiers varying widely in reported AUC and external validation remaining limited [R55]; in reproductive immunology, integrative analyses of recurrent pregnancy loss still depend on borrowed frameworks such as WGCNA, MOFA and bespoke deep-learning classifiers rather than purpose-built tools [R53]. A recent community roadmap emphasises that microbiome multi-omics is held back less by the absence of algorithms than by the lack of standardised workflows, benchmarked datasets and FAIR-compliant pipelines [R54].

Within this landscape, EasyMultiProfiler is presented as an R-based multi-omics workflow for microbiome research that uses SummarizedExperiment and MultiAssayExperiment as unifying data structures and is organised around five named modules—extraction, preparation, support, analysis and visualisation—to standardise integration and improve reproducibility, as illustrated on human and mouse host–microbiome cohorts [R1]. Its documented focus on the Bioconductor ecosystem and on model-organism host–microbiome pairs differentiates it from gNOMO/gNOMO2's emphasis on non-model hosts [R21, R34], though this specialisation constrains rather than broadens its applicability. The EasyMultiProfiler description does not specify which operations are implemented within each of the five modules, nor does it document behaviour on non-model host microbiomes, on dynamic or longitudinal designs, or on integration scenarios beyond the human/mouse gut cohorts used in the original demonstration [R1].

A candid assessment is warranted at the field level rather than at the level of any single tool. Microbiome-centred tools still suffer from severe annotation bottlenecks: functional inference for metagenomes and especially metatranscriptomes and metaproteomes remains database-bound, and strain-level ambiguity means that nominally identical species can encode different functions across cohorts. No microbiome-native gold-standard benchmark with known ground-truth interactions is currently available, and head-to-head statistical comparisons against MOFA, mixOmics-DIABLO, SNF or graph-neural-network alternatives are absent not only for EasyMultiProfiler [R1] but for gNOMO2 [R21], PALM [R31] and the broader microbiome-integration class; benchmarking infrastructure that none of these tools provide remains the field's most pressing gap. Dynamic-modelling approaches such as PALM [R31] address complementary problems and cannot be substituted by static-integration pipelines. Until microbiome-native evaluation infrastructure becomes available, claims of superiority among microbiome integration tools should be read with caution, and the field would benefit less from yet another statistical engine than from shared evaluation infrastructure.

Web servers and point-and-click platforms represent the most accessible tier of multi-omics software, packaging analytical workflows behind graphical interfaces that shield users from command-line installation overhead. Profiler [R10] offers one of the broader analytic spans among the surveyed web platforms, providing a Streamlit-based environment that spans QC, preprocessing, statistical testing, machine and deep learning, biomarker discovery, pathway and drug-target enrichment, and survival modeling across proteomics, transcriptomics, lipidomics and other modalities, deployable as web or desktop application. ExpOmics [R49] is similarly broad, offering seven applications and four toolkits with twenty-eight customizable functions for differential expression, co-expression, WGCNA, feature selection and enrichment across mRNAs, lncRNAs, miRNAs, circRNAs, piRNAs and proteins without organism restriction. ExpressVis [R30] foregrounds biologist-oriented interactivity, organising differential expression, clustering, survival analysis and integration with protein–protein interaction networks and pathway maps into six modules. CFViSA [R50] integrates dedicated microbiome and transcriptome pipelines alongside seventy-nine analysis tools and includes didactic features such as a demonstration course and task history interface, illustrating how accessibility and training are increasingly bundled into platform design.

A second category consists of platform "ecosystems" that distribute multi-omics functionality across interlinked but specialised web servers. The Analyst suite [R15] is the paradigmatic example, combining ExpressAnalyst and MetaboAnalyst for single-omics processing of transcriptomics/proteomics and lipidomics data, OmicsNet for knowledge-driven integration through biological networks, and OmicsAnalyst for data-driven integration through joint dimensionality reduction; the protocol walks users through these stages on a human pancreatic islet and plasma cohort. MOPAW [R26] targets the Cancer Genomics Cloud and exposes Multivariate Single Sample Gene Set Analysis (MOGSA) through a point-and-click interface, automating data preparation, dimensionality reduction and pathway analysis across CNA, transcriptomics, proteomics and phosphoproteomics data. The single-cell analyst [R14] provides automated QC, processing, phenotype analysis and over twenty interactive visualisation tools across six single-cell omics types (scRNA-seq, scATAC-seq, scImmune profiling, scCNV, CyTOF, flow cytometry) and spatial transcriptomics, deployable both online and offline.

A third category privileges network-based visual reasoning. MONGKIE [R37], an early Java-based entry, integrates network visualisation with omics data analysis tools for interactive visual mining of TCGA glioblastoma multi-omics layers. PhenoMultiOmics [R22] narrows the network concept to enzymatic reactions, curating cancer-gene–protein–metabolite relationships and visualising perturbed reaction-induced multi-omics networks with biomarker discovery via differential expression and pathway enrichment. NOODAI [R43] generalises the idea by constructing joint interaction networks from representative per-omics traits and applying the MONET decomposition tool to identify disease-relevant modules. These platforms trade methodological novelty for interpretability: anchoring interpretation in curated biological graphs reduces dependence on statistical sophistication but inherits the biases and incompleteness of those knowledge bases.

A fourth hybrid class fuses pre-curated public repositories with analysis modules, becoming searchable atlases with built-in statistics. SportsXbiodata [R38] aggregates 2,563 public multi-omics exercise datasets and 3,600 publications, providing expression profiling, immune infiltration, phenotype-gene correlation, knowledge graph and enrichment analyses, with free access. LOSTdb [R46] integrates 295 lung-cancer multi-omics datasets with curated metadata and modules for subtype annotation, cross-search and integrated analysis. These resources are valuable for re-use, but the analytical methods offered within them tend to be conservative, reflecting the need to operate on heterogeneous, partially standardised input data of variable provenance.

This proliferation of interfaces, however, should not be confused with methodological diversity. Five caveats are worth stating explicitly. (1) The word "unified" in many platform descriptions papers over the fact that the underlying logic is often concatenation of single-omics tools rather than joint modelling; Profiler [R10] presents an extensive menu that nonetheless relies on modality-specific QC and analysis pathways stitched together at the user-interface level. The Analyst suite [R15] is more transparent in this regard, formally distinguishing knowledge-driven network integration from data-driven dimensionality-reduction integration, yet even its data-driven arm depends on algorithms (PCA-, PLS- and sparse-PLS-based embeddings) that pre-date the current generation of variational factorisations [R4], matrix factorisation with transfer learning [R42], and contrastive deep methods [R40]. (2) Web platforms systematically hide preprocessing choices from the user, which is helpful for novices but problematic for analysts who need to evaluate how filtering, normalisation and batch handling propagate downstream; the closed pipelines of MOPAW [R26] and PhenoMultiOmics [R22] offer little room to swap in alternative strategies, in contrast to containerised workflow frameworks such as the FAIR Digital Object pipeline for childhood externalising behaviour multi-omics [R18], which exposes its dependencies via Nextflow with version-pinned containers. (3) Most web platforms lag behind the algorithmic state of the art, neither implementing MOFA+-style scalable variational inference [R4] nor the rapidly expanding family of graph neural network integrators such as MO-GCAN [R39], MODA [R44] or BioNeuralNet [R8]; MOPAW [R26] and the Analyst suite's data-driven arm [R15] are partial exceptions, exposing MOGSA and joint dimensionality reduction respectively. (4) Network-oriented servers such as NOODAI [R43] and PhenoMultiOmics [R22] expose interpretable visual artefacts, but the underlying network priors and edge-weighting schemes are rarely benchmarked against each other, making it unclear whether observed modules reflect biology or curation bias. (5) The abundance of platforms can mask a shortage of cross-platform standards for input formats, metadata and reporting, so users face substantial friction when moving between resources; reproducibility infrastructure in particular varies across container formats (Docker, Singularity/Apptainer, Conda) and is rarely documented at the level of re-execution success on independent hardware. Taken together, web servers and GUI workflows play a substantial role in democratising multi-omics, but their rapid numerical growth is not, by itself, evidence of methodological progress.

Network-based and deep learning approaches have become the most rapidly expanding family of methods for multi-omics integration because they explicitly encode relationships among features and learn joint representations end-to-end. The lineage begins with similarity network fusion, which constructs per-data-type patient similarity networks and iteratively fuses them into a single integrated graph for cancer subtyping and survival prediction across mRNA, DNA methylation and miRNA [R5]. This patient-similarity paradigm inspired a wave of follow-up tools, and a recent unification of statistical meta-analysis with similarity-network-fusion-style integration has been demonstrated for IPF transcriptomic meta-analysis and THP-1 macrophage multi-omics data [R6], suggesting that network thinking is no longer confined to a single method but increasingly serves as an interoperability layer across analytical pipelines. Together, these works established that pairwise similarity matrices, once fused, provide a basis for subtyping on the cancer cohorts in which they were demonstrated, and they set the conceptual template for the methods that followed.

Graph neural networks (GNNs) extend this logic by treating omics features or patients as nodes and learning low-dimensional embeddings through message passing. BioNeuralNet, a modular Python framework, exposes a unified API for network construction, GNN-based representation learning and downstream scikit-learn- and PyTorch-compatible tasks on gene, protein and metabolite graphs [R8]; the ArXiv preprint of the same tool is available as [R12]. Cancer-focused GNN frameworks have proliferated rapidly: DeepMoIC combines autoencoders, patient-similarity networks and deep graph convolutions, with pan-cancer subtyping reported as its principal task [R19]; LAGProg augments biological networks with a conditional variational autoencoder to overcome the limited connectivity of curated pathways in prognosis prediction [R24]; MO-GCAN pairs graph convolutions with attention across eight cancer types [R39]; and MODA maps omics features onto a curated knowledge graph and reports advantages over seven existing integration methods on classification tasks [R44]. CrossIsoFun specialises the GNN paradigm to isoform function prediction by combining GCN classifiers with a View Correlation Discovery Network to exploit isoform–isoform interactions [R47]. Collectively, these architectures demonstrate the flexibility of graph-based learning but, as discussed below, almost uniformly report metrics on cancer panels drawn from TCGA and related resources, with few examples tested on non-malignant phenotypes, longitudinal sampling designs or microbiome–host systems.

A complementary thread replaces fixed graph topology with learned attention. MOADLN applies per-omics self-attention followed by a Multi-omics Correlation Discovery Network to fuse mRNA, methylation and miRNA [R23]; MODILM uses Graph Attention Networks combined with MLPs and a View Correlation Discovery Network for complex disease classification [R52]. These attention-based designs report improvements over simple concatenation in the input or feature space on the demonstrated benchmarks, but they inherit the same evaluation regime as the GNN family — accuracy/AUROC/F1 on cancer panels is the typical headline — and almost no assessment is provided of how attention weights map to biologically interpretable molecular events. A separate image-style branch converts omics matrices into 2-D images: a representative method embeds gene expression, methylation and copy-number alteration via UMAP, paints them as RGB channels and trains a convolutional neural network on the resulting images to predict Gleason score and tumour stage [R29]. While conceptually elegant and effective on the demonstrated cohorts, this image-pipeline paradigm imposes an additional inductive bias — pixel adjacency becomes meaningful — for which there is no biological justification, and whose generalisation beyond prostate and breast cancer remains untested in the cited evidence.

A third stream couples deep architectures with contrastive or generative objectives rather than explicit attention. CAEncoder combines a Vision Transformer encoder with a CycleGAN generator in a contrastive end-to-end pipeline for cancer detection [R40], exemplifying designs that align modalities through adversarial training and reconstruction rather than through attention-weighted fusion.

A fourth stream embeds prior-knowledge networks and Bayesian regularisation directly into the integration step. NetMIM uses a spike-and-slab prior over pathway structure and a data-augmentation scheme to handle block-wise missingness for biomarker selection and outcome prediction [R20]; MINGLE performs sparse network estimation across omics layers followed by integrated visualisation for glioma heterogeneity [R41]; and the NOODAI web server constructs joint interaction networks from representative per-omics traits and decomposes them with the MONET algorithm to surface disease-relevant modules [R43]. These methods are more transparent than end-to-end deep models, but the cited evidence does not document stress tests of prior-strength choices or missing-data imputation against realistic null or confounded scenarios. In practice, the line between deep learning with a graph prior and a network-based Bayesian model is increasingly blurred, yet the evaluation standards remain strikingly similar across both.

Despite their methodological diversity, these approaches share three structural weaknesses. First, headline performance is reported almost exclusively on TCGA-derived cancer panels, leaving open whether the gains transfer to non-malignant disease, longitudinal cohorts or microbiome–host settings where sample sizes are smaller, batch effects more pronounced and confounders more pervasive. Second, interpretability is asserted rather than measured: attention weights, GNN message-passing scores and UMAP pixel coordinates are presented as explanations without systematic benchmarks against biological ground truth, perturbation data or expert clinician evaluation, and ablation studies that selectively remove supposedly important nodes are the exception rather than the rule. Third, predictive uncertainty is rarely exposed; an exception is TMODINET, which couples self-attentional and graph dynamic learning with a Dirichlet-based uncertainty head for cancer diagnosis [R16], but even this framework evaluates trustworthiness only on classification accuracy and does not, in the cited abstract, document calibration drift across cohorts, behaviour under distribution shift or comparisons against Bayesian or conformal baselines. In the absence of standardised interpretability and uncertainty benchmarks, the consistently strong classification numbers produced by network and deep-learning methods should be read as evidence of architectural flexibility and capacity to fit curated cancer panels rather than as a demonstration of clinical or biological readiness — and, as observed across the integration literature more broadly, no head-to-head, multi-domain benchmark has, to our knowledge, been published against which these claims could be jointly evaluated.

EasyMultiProfiler (EMP) is an R-based workflow for multi-omics integration in microbiome research, built around the SummarizedExperiment and MultiAssayExperiment classes that have become the de facto Bioconductor standard for coordinating heterogeneous assays [R1, R36]. Its documented architecture spans five interconnected modules — data extraction, preparation, support, analysis and visualisation — and is illustrated on human and mouse gut microbiome cohorts with matched host multi-omics data [R1]. By committing to MultiAssayExperiment as the unifying container, EMP inherits a data structure that has already been validated for coordinated storage and manipulation of multi-assay experiments, including TCGA cancer resources [R36] and curated single-cell multimodal landmark datasets [R51], so that operations such as subsetting by sample, joining across modalities and propagating metadata are inherited rather than reinvented. Whether the module decomposition corresponds to a natural-language or biology-oriented workflow syntax, or specifically embeds microbiome-targeted quality control, taxonomic aggregation and pathway mapping, is not characterised in the available description [R1]; the discussion is therefore restricted to what the source documents.

Several features differentiate EMP from neighbouring microbiome pipelines. Microbiome-centred tools such as gNOMO and gNOMO2 target community-level meta-omics integration through Snakemake and Nextflow workflows, respectively, and have been benchmarked on dedicated metagenomic, metatranscriptomic and metaproteomic datasets [R34, R21]; PALM aligns multi-omics time-series data and applies dynamic Bayesian networks for longitudinal inference, including host–microbiome contexts [R31]; and timeOmics extends a Bioconductor-style framework to longitudinal integration across microbiome and host layers [R27]. EMP's documented scope is to couple microbiome profiling with host-side omics within a single MultiAssayExperiment container, which gNOMO and gNOMO2 also pursue, but from workflow managers tailored for non-model organisms [R1, R34, R21]. gNOMO2's own description indicates that its differential-abundance, integration and visualisation modules are benchmarked on four datasets [R21], so the standard applied here — illustration rather than head-to-head comparison — is field-wide rather than tool-specific.

The principal design choices of EMP are best appreciated by comparing them with the broader landscape. Generic factor-analytic frameworks such as MOFA [R2] and MOFA+ [R4] are inferential engines that operate on matrices or tensors and infer shared and modality-specific latent factors; mixOmics provides multivariate PLS-based machinery for dimension reduction, feature selection and integrative analysis [R3], with DIABLO implementing a multi-block discriminant extension [R35]. Network-based approaches such as Similarity Network Fusion construct per-data-type patient similarity networks and fuse them into a single integrated network for subtyping and survival prediction [R5]; Bayesian alternatives such as NetMIM handle block missingness via data augmentation [R20]. Whether MOFA's factor inference generalises to the highly skewed, zero-inflated distributions typical of microbiome relative-abundance matrices, and whether the assumptions of similarity-network fusion and factor analysis can be empirically distinguished under microbiome conditions, are, to our knowledge, untested in the cited literature. EMP's reported positioning is to host analytical components within a microbiome-aware R workflow rather than to compete on factor or network methodology per se [R1].

The limitations need to be stated candidly. The published evidence base for EMP is concentrated on human and mouse gut microbiome cohorts, and its documented advantages are demonstrated primarily through illustrative applications rather than head-to-head statistical benchmarking against MOFA, mixOmics-DIABLO, SNF, MLMF or graph-neural-network alternatives [R1, R13, R19, R39]. The same caveat applies across the surveyed landscape: MLMF is benchmarked on twelve multi-omics datasets [R13], MOADLN on TCGA cancer cohorts [R23], DeepMoIC on pan-cancer data [R19], and gNOMO2 on four datasets [R21]. Within EMP specifically, the available description does not enumerate uncertainty quantification, model selection or statistical inference procedures, nor does it document a re-execution benchmark on heterogeneous infrastructure; these are gaps the source itself does not close [R1], so the reproducibility standard this review demands of other tools applies with equal force to EMP. EMP does not target single-cell or spatial multi-omics, which single-cell analyst [R14], the multi-omics prediction and integration benchmark [R17], CelLink [R45] and the scRNA/scATAC integration benchmark [R48] explicitly address; these are scope boundaries rather than competitive gaps. Likewise, EMP is not presented as a deep-learning platform with cloud execution, in contrast to dedicated platforms such as MOPAW on the Cancer Genomics Cloud [R26] or to web-based ecosystems such as the Analyst suite [R15], Profiler [R10], ExpOmics [R49], PhenoMultiOmics [R22], NOODAI [R43] and CFViSA [R50]; EMP is also not positioned within automated pipeline-construction or workflow-provenance frameworks of the kind offered by moiraine [R7] or by the Nextflow Research Object Crate exemplar [R18].

The MOFA family deserves a specific note. The original MOFA [R2] and MOFA+ [R4] are the formulations whose evidence base this review considers; MOFA2, the actively maintained successor with a distinct implementation and broader adoption, is not represented in the cited cards and is therefore out of scope here. Whether claims derived from the original MOFA formulation transfer to its successor and to microbiome settings is an open question that the available evidence does not resolve.

In practical terms, EMP's documented strengths — its use of MultiAssayExperiment as the unifying container, the explicit five-module decomposition, and the host–microbiome focus — give it a specific niche among microbiome workflows, while the evidence base for these claims remains concentrated on human and mouse gut datasets [R1]. What the evidence does not yet show is that EMP's analytical components outperform competing factorisation, network or deep-learning methods under controlled benchmarking, that they generalise beyond gut microbial communities, or that they scale to the regime of modern single-cell and spatial multi-omics. Treating EMP as a microbiome-specialised workflow layer that interoperates with — rather than supplants — these specialised methods is consistent with the current evidence base.
